meta.title: Who really said "These books ain't window dressing. I think Machiavelli's the most sophisticated writer outside of Shakespeare"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine. Tyson said it to Paul Hayward in a Maui pre-fight session, printed in The Daily Telegraph on 1 May 2002 — and it is only the first half of what he said.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'These books ain't window dressing. I think Machiavelli's the most sophisticated writer outside of Shakespeare'?
meta.ogDescription: Really Mike Tyson — to Paul Hayward for The Daily Telegraph, 1 May 2002, before the Lennox Lewis fight. The answer runs on for three more sentences.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and unusually well documented for a Tyson line. He said it to reporters in his beach chalet on Maui, and Paul Hayward printed it in The Daily Telegraph on 1 May 2002 under the headline “Boxing: Tyson’s complicated world.” The two sentences people search for are the opening of a longer answer — the transcript runs on for three more, and the quote sites generally do carry all five.

source.heading: The interview it comes from

docMeta.dd: Paul Hayward, filing from Maui, Hawaii
Machiavelli in Hell, named in the article as one of Tyson’s “current books for the beach”

source.excerpt: “That’s entertainment for me. These books ain’t window dressing. I think Machiavelli’s the most sophisticated writer outside of Shakespeare. Way ahead of his time. Such a manipulative person. Everything he accomplished he did by kissin’ ass.”
trail: 1 May 2002 — the primary source. Paul Hayward’s Telegraph piece ↗ carries the sentence verbatim, inside a longer answer, in a report datelined from Tyson’s Maui chalet ahead of his fight with Lennox Lewis in Memphis on 8 June.

Wikiquote points at the same article. The Mike Tyson page ↗ files the quote under “On literature” and links it to the Telegraph URL — a bare link rather than a full citation, but it resolves to the right piece.
Quote sites split on sourcing. AZQuotes ↗ credits it to the Hayward interview of 1 May 2002; other listings reprint the same words with no publication or date attached at all.

The book Tyson was actually holding. Machiavelli in Hell, the title Hayward names, is Sebastian de Grazia’s 1989 biography ↗, which won the 1990 Pulitzer Prize for Biography or Autobiography — a life of Machiavelli, not The Prince itself.
source.excerptNote: Hayward sets the scene before the quote: Tyson on a sofa in a Hawaiian beach chalet, a stack of Machiavelli behind his head on the window sill, browsing racing pigeons on a laptop. The reporter notes that Machiavelli in Hell was among the books, then gives Tyson the floor. The “window dressing” line is a rebuttal — Hayward records in the same paragraph that some people treated Tyson’s reading as a long-running ruse.

author.name: Mike Tyson
author.heading: Who said it
author.metaLine: Born 30 June 1966 · American boxer; held the WBC, WBA and IBF heavyweight titles simultaneously
author.bio: Born in Brooklyn on 30 June 1966, Tyson finished his professional career with 50 wins — 44 by knockout — against 7 losses and 2 no contests, and at his peak held the WBC, WBA and IBF heavyweight belts at the same time. He also read, conspicuously and combatively: interviewers found him surrounded by books and happy to argue about them. The Maui session that produced this line was a build-up to a bad night — on 8 June 2002 in Memphis, Lennox Lewis knocked him out in the eighth round.

misattribution.heading: What gets lost in transit
misattribution.intro: Mike Tyson is one of the internet’s favourite pegs for invented wisdom, so the first instinct with a line this quotable is to doubt it. This one survives the test — it is on the record, bylined and dated. What goes wrong is everything around it.

items.why: Compilations reprint the sentence with no publication, no date and no interviewer — The Fight City’s list ↗ and QuoteStats ↗ both carry it bare. A real quote with no source is one repost away from being treated as a fake.

The form people look it up in — the form at the top of this page — stops at “Shakespeare.” The reprints are better than that: Wikiquote ↗, AZQuotes ↗ and the listicles all carry the full five sentences. But read only the first two and it is a straight compliment; read to the end and Machiavelli is “such a manipulative person” who got everything “by kissin’ ass.” See the full passage ↗

It was not a reflective aside — it was said to a room of sceptical reporters at a pre-fight press session on Maui, printed ahead of the Lennox Lewis bout in Memphis on 8 June 2002, and aimed squarely at people who thought the book stack was a prop. Hayward’s report ↗ makes the scepticism explicit.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: really Mike Tyson, on the record, to Paul Hayward of The Daily Telegraph, 1 May 2002 ↗ — and the full answer is three sentences longer, and sharper, than the two people search for.

context.heading: Why it landed
lead: The setting is the whole joke. Tyson is on a sofa in a Hawaiian beach chalet, looking at racing pigeons on a laptop, with a pile of Machiavelli on the window sill behind his head. A group of reporters have flown in to write about a heavyweight fight, and what they get is fifty minutes of monologue taking in American literature, betrayal and Jesus Christ. Hayward’s article records the room’s open scepticism — the suspicion that the reading was a long-running act — and the “window dressing” line is Tyson answering it directly.

What makes the quote stick is that it is not really a compliment. Read the rest of it and Machiavelli comes out as a flatterer who got everything by “kissin’ ass” — a fairly Machiavellian reading of Machiavelli, and a pointed thing to say to a press corps you have just accused of writing you up as a monster for money.
detailsBody: The same answer ran on into a list of favourites — Fitzgerald, Hemingway, Tolstoy, Pushkin, Mailer — with the observation that the greats are all connected, each admiring the one before. Hayward transcribes it in the Telegraph article ↗.

The Machiavelli on the pile was Machiavelli in Hell, which the article names by title. That is Sebastian de Grazia’s 1989 book ↗, a Pulitzer-winning biography rather than a copy of The Prince — a detail that quietly supports Tyson’s point about the books not being decoration.
The fight the interview was previewing went badly: on 8 June 2002 in Memphis, Lennox Lewis knocked Tyson out in the eighth round.
context.pull: A stack of Machiavelli on the window sill, a laptop full of racing pigeons, and a heavyweight daring the room to call it a pose.
